To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we introduce the novel LAF architecture, which is a learnable aggregator of sets of arbitrary cardinalities.
we propose LAF, a learnable aggregator that can approximate several extensively  used aggregators as well as more  complex  functions.
LAF outperforms state of the art methods on semi-syntheic and real world datasets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
learning the aggregation function for sets.
the question whether it is possible to learn a universal aggregator over sets of variable cardinality, and if yes, how to do so efficiently.
the question of whether it is possible to learn aggregation functions over sets, and if so, what is the best way to do it.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our proposed LAF  is a powerful, flexible, and easy to use aggregator for sets, and that it outperforms state of the art approaches on several tasks.
LAF outperforms the other methods in most of the considered scenarios, with the exception of a few cases where it is not able to outperform the other methods.
the LAF model is the first model that can learn arbitrary set aggregation functions and outperforms all existing approaches.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show the importance of the choice of the aggregator for the learning task, and that a learnable aggregator is able to outperform the standard choices.
learning aggregation functions can lead to better representations for learning on sets.
LAF can learn a variety of set aggregators with a single model and outperforms the state-of-the-art on several set learning tasks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
learning aggregation functions for sets can be more powerful than fixed functions and can be easily incorporated into existing neural architectures.
, by using LAF, we can learn to aggregate sets without relying on a pre-fixed function.
, when learning aggregation functions, it is better to learn a function that approximates the desired function, rather than learning a function that decomposes the desired function.
